title: Periodic table structure and blocks; Ionisation energies
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: PT01#t1 term and clue written for the game; PT01#t3 term and clue written for the game; AS05#t3 term and clue written for the game; PT01#t4 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AS05#N.4a, PT01#N.6, AS05#N.7a, PT01#N.12a, AS05#N.10a, AS05#N.11.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Period
items.clue: A row of the table; its number gives the outer occupied shell.

items.label: Valence electrons
items.clue: The outer-shell particles of an atom: seven for bromine, 4s² 4p⁵.

items.label: Convergence limit
items.clue: Where hydrogen's lines for falls to n = 1 crowd together at high frequency.

items.label: Metalloid
items.clue: Element on the stepped line, such as B, Si or Ge, with in-between properties.

questions.stem: Which equation represents the second ionisation energy of calcium?

options.text: Ca⁺(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + e⁻
Ca(g) → Ca²⁺(g) + 2e⁻
Ca⁺(aq) → Ca²⁺(aq) + e⁻
Ca(s) → Ca²⁺(g) + 2e⁻

questions.explanation: One mole of electrons removed from one mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

questions.stem: Germanium is in period 4, group 14. Which is the full electron configuration of a germanium atom?

options.text: 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s² 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d² 4s²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p²
1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d¹⁰ 4s² 4p⁴

questions.explanation: Period 4, p-block: fill up to 4p. Group 14 gives 14 − 10 = 4 valence electrons, 4s² 4p². With the 3d¹⁰, the total is 32 electrons.

questions.stem: How does the first ionisation energy generally change across Period 3 from sodium to argon, and why?

options.text: It decreases, as the fixed pull of the nucleus is shared among more and more electrons.
It decreases, as the atoms get larger because more electrons are added along the period.
It increases, as atoms closer to a full outer shell resist losing any of their outer electrons.
It increases, as the nuclear charge rises while the outer electrons have similar shielding.

questions.explanation: Nuclear charge +11 to +18; the electron removed is in the third shell, with similar shielding. 496 → 1521 kJ mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Beryllium, 1s² 2s², and helium, 1s², both have two electrons in their outer s sub-shell. Why is beryllium placed in group 2, but helium in group 18?

options.text: Beryllium is a solid and helium is a gas, and group 18 holds the gaseous elements.
Beryllium has four electrons and helium two, and the group number counts the total.
Beryllium's 2s² electrons are in a higher shell, so they are inner electrons, not valence electrons.
Beryllium's outer shell, n = 2, is far from full, while helium's n = 1 shell is full with just two.

questions.stem: The first four successive ionisation energies of an element X are 578, 1817, 2745 and 11 577 kJ mol⁻¹. How many electrons does an atom of X have in its outer shell?

options.text: Four, as the large increase appears at the fourth ionisation energy
One, as the second value is already over three times larger than the first
Three, as the large increase comes after the third electron is removed
Thirteen, as X has atomic number 13

questions.explanation: 578 → 1817 → 2745 rise steadily; then the fourth is about four times the third. Three outer electrons: X is aluminium.

questions.stem: Element X is in Period 3. Its first six ionisation energies are 1012, 1907, 2914, 4964, 6274 and 21 268 kJ mol⁻¹. Which statement identifies X and explains the large sixth value?

options.text: X is sulfur: the jump is at the sixth ionisation energy, so X has six outer electrons.
X is phosphorus: the sixth electron is the first from the second shell, nearer the nucleus.
X is phosphorus: the sixth electron would come from a full shell, which is especially stable.
X is aluminium: the rise from 2914 to 4964 is where a new shell starts.

questions.explanation: Five electrons come from the third shell. The sixth comes from 2p: much closer to the nucleus, much less shielded, so held far more strongly.
